notes.meaning: Ezekiel's heavenly guide brings him back to the temple doors, where water flows eastward from beneath the entrance. The stream runs along the south side of the altar, showing that this life-giving flow starts right at God's dwelling place. The temple had no natural spring, so this water is a miraculous gift from the Lord.

differ.view: Understand the river as a spiritual picture of the gospel and the Holy Spirit flowing out to bless the world through Christ and His church.
Expect a literal river to flow from a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem during a future earthly reign of Christ.

notes.meaning: Because the outer eastern gate was shut, the guide leads Ezekiel around through the north gate to the outside. There the prophet spots the water trickling out from the south side of the eastern gate. The stream begins as just a quiet, tiny trickle.

The guide walks eastward with a measuring cord and measures off about a third of a mile. He leads Ezekiel across the stream, and the water reaches Ezekiel's ankles. God begins this mighty work in a small, gentle way.

The guide measures another third of a mile, and the water rises to Ezekiel's knees. He measures the same distance again, and the river is now up to Ezekiel's waist. The stream grows deeper simply by flowing forward, without any other creeks joining it.

After measuring one more distance, the stream becomes a river too deep to walk across. Ezekiel can only cross it by swimming. This sudden, miraculous growth shows how God's blessings expand far beyond anything human strength can measure.

The guide asks Ezekiel if he has taken close notice of this extraordinary wonder. Then he leads the prophet back along the bank of the river. God wants His people to pause and pay careful attention to the greatness of what He is doing.

When Ezekiel returns to the river's edge, he sees many flourishing trees on both banks. Where there was once dry and barren ground, God's water has produced abundant life. The Lord brings fruitfulness wherever His presence reaches.

The guide explains that the river flows eastward down into the Jordan valley and empties into the Dead Sea. The Dead Sea is so salty that nothing can live in it, but this river makes its water completely fresh and healthy. God's presence brings life and healing into places ruined by death and decay.

Swarms of living creatures and great schools of fish will thrive wherever this river flows. The fresh water washes away the salt and bitterness, transforming a lifeless sea into a place teeming with activity. God's grace brings true spiritual life wherever it goes.

Fishermen will line the shores of the once-dead sea from En-gedi in the south to En-eglaim in the north, drying and spreading their nets. The sea will hold as many kinds of fish as the Mediterranean Sea. What was once completely barren will become busy and fruitful.

The marshes and swamps near the sea will not be turned into fresh water, but will stay salty. This preserved the salt that people needed for seasoning food and preserving meat. It also reminds readers that those who refuse God's healing remain barren.

Fruit trees of all kinds will grow along both banks of the river, never losing their leaves or running out of fruit. They will produce a fresh crop every single month because the water feeding them comes straight from the sanctuary. The fruit gives nourishing food, and the leaves provide medicine for healing.

The Lord announces the borders for dividing the land among the twelve tribes of Israel. Joseph is granted two shares, which went to the tribes of his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. This honored the ancient promise Jacob gave to Joseph when blessing his family.

The land is to be shared equally among the tribes because the Lord promised it to their ancestors by a solemn oath. No tribe was to be left out or pushed aside in the restored community. God keeps His promises to His people, even after long seasons of exile.

The northern boundary starts at the Mediterranean Sea and runs eastward through Lebanon and Syria toward Damascus, ending at Hazar-enan. This line marks out the northern edge of the promised inheritance. It shows that God's plan provides a clearly defined and secure homeland for His people.

The eastern border runs south between Damascus and Hauran, following the Jordan River between Gilead and Israel down to the Dead Sea as far as Tamar. It sets the Jordan River as the border, focusing the inheritance on the land of Canaan proper. God gives His people a clear place to call home.

The southern border runs from Tamar westward to the oasis of Kadesh, and follows the Brook of Egypt out to the Mediterranean Sea. This matches the southern border God gave Israel through Moses before they entered the land. The Lord remains faithful to His original covenant boundaries.

The western border is the Great Sea, known today as the Mediterranean Sea, running all the way north to a point across from Lebo-hamath. The coastline serves as a natural barrier enclosing the land. God establishes safe and visible borders for His restored nation.

Ezekiel is told to divide this entire region among the tribes of Israel according to the borders just given. All twelve tribes are reunited as one people under God, putting an end to past divisions. The Lord restores true unity among His people.

Foreigners who live permanently among the Israelites and raise families are granted land rights just like native-born citizens. Whichever tribe a foreigner lives in, that tribe must assign him a permanent piece of land. Under older laws, foreigners were protected but could not own tribal land, so this generous command points to God welcoming people from all nations into His family.
